screens.title: Events and Logging
screens.subtitle: How contracts speak to the outside world without bloating on-chain storage

narration.text: Today you will learn how Solidity events let a contract publish concise, permanent notifications that external applications can read. Events write entries to the transaction log — a cheaper, append-only ledger optimized for search — and are the principal mechanism for off-chain communication from a smart contract. You'll see why events are gas-efficient compared to storing data in state, how to declare and emit them, and why indexing matters for filtering. We will ground these ideas with concrete examples like Deposit, Withdrawal, and Transfer events, and a remix-based activity that adds Transfer and Approval to a token contract. Importantly, you'll learn common safety rules: do not emit sensitive data, don't expect on-chain contracts to read logs, and balance indexing against gas cost. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to decide when to emit an event, how to structure its parameters for efficient queries, and how off-chain listeners use topics and data to reconstruct contract activity. Keep an eye out for a practical exercise you can run in Remix to see event logs appear in the transaction console.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Events are the efficient, off-chain bridge from your contract to user interfaces, explorers, and analytics tools; they log actions cheaply and in a searchable way.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: In this chapter you'll acquire a set of practical skills for using events in Solidity. First, you'll be able to declare and emit events in a contract and recognize when an event is the right tool versus on-chain storage. Second, you'll understand how indexed parameters change the way events are stored and queried, and you'll learn how to decide which fields to index to balance searchability with gas costs. Third, you'll implement events in real functions so that your contract notifies the outside world when important actions occur. Finally, you'll learn how external tools and dApps subscribe to topics and parse event data to present timely updates. Each objective focuses on both the how and the why, so you can use events effectively in UI updates, analytics pipelines, and off-chain triggers while avoiding privacy and cost pitfalls.

screens.title: What is an Event?
screens.subtitle: Definition, transaction logs, and why events exist

narration.text: An event in Solidity is a declared, named structure that a contract can emit to record an occurrence in the transaction log. Think of events as immutable broadcast messages that live in the transaction's log rather than in contract storage. They are cheaper to write than state because logs are optimized for storage size and searchability, and they were designed specifically for off-chain systems to observe contract behavior. For example, a Deposit event with the depositor address and amount tells UIs and analytics tools that funds arrived, without permanently storing that record in the contract's state variables. A common misconception is to treat events as a substitute for on-chain state; they are not. Other contracts cannot read event data, and you should not rely on them for on-chain logic. Instead, use events to notify external listeners about significant actions, such as transfers, approvals, or ownership changes. Remember, events provide a verifiable, timestamped trail and are valuable for debugging, auditing, and driving UX updates. To check your understanding: when would you choose an event over updating a public state variable, and why?

keyIdea.title: Event definition
keyIdea.text: Events are log entries emitted by contracts to inform off-chain systems; they are cheaper than state but not readable on-chain.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › What is an Event?
Definition

Event as a log record

Events emit a permanent log entry during a transaction. Logs are cheaper than on-chain state and intended for off-chain consumption.

Concrete example
A Deposit event includes the depositor address and amount. When the contract emits it, wallets and UIs can update balances without reading contract storage.
Common misconception
Events are not a substitute for state: contracts cannot read logs and you must not rely on events for on-chain logic.
Teaching visual
Transaction Log
Append-only, indexed topics and data payloads. Cheaper than storing everything in state.
When to use
  • Notify UIs of state changes
  • Emit audit trails and analytics events
  • Trigger off-chain services
Key Takeaway
Use events to broadcast contract actions to off-chain listeners; keep sensitive data out of logs.

screens.title: Declare and Emit — Syntax and Patterns
screens.subtitle: How to write event declarations and emit them correctly

narration.text: Declaring events in Solidity uses the event keyword followed by the name and a parameter list. For example, a Deposit event might be declared as Deposit(address indexed sender, uint amount). Indexed marks parameters you want searchable in topics. You emit events inside functions using the emit keyword after any important checks and state updates; emitting before successful completion risks logging failed or reverted actions. A concrete pattern is to perform require checks first, update state, then emit the event. For example, in a deposit function you check conditions, increase an internal balance mapping, and then emit Deposit with the sender and value. Another common pattern is to emit OwnershipTransferred after updating the owner variable, passing both the prior owner and the new owner. A common mistake is emitting sensitive or large data structures — logs are public and cost gas. Also remember there are limits: three indexed parameters per event plus the signature topic. When you design an event, pick meaningful, minimal fields: indexed keys you will filter by, and non-indexed payload for extra details. This disciplined approach keeps gas manageable and makes logs useful for consumers.

keyIdea.title: Declaration pattern
keyIdea.text: Declare events with indexed searchable keys and emit them after successful state changes to provide reliable off-chain notifications.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Declare & Emit
Syntax
// Declare events
event Deposit(address indexed sender, uint amount);
event OwnershipTransferred(address indexed previousOwner, address indexed newOwner);

// Emit inside a function after checks and state updates
emit Deposit(msg.sender, msg.value);
emit OwnershipTransferred(oldOwner, _newOwner);
Keep declarations concise and place larger or private fields in non-indexed parameters or avoid logging them entirely.
Patterns
Emit after state change
Perform require checks and update state before emitting to avoid misleading logs.
Index only keys you need
Limit indexed parameters to those you will realistically filter by.
Common mistake
Emitting sensitive user data in logs is public and irreversible.
Key Takeaway
Design events for efficient queries and emit them only when the transaction succeeds.

screens.title: Emit Events in Functions — Safe Placement
screens.subtitle: Where to place emit so logs reflect committed state

narration.text: When you emit an event, place that emit after successful checks and after you update any state your event describes. This ensures the logged information matches what the contract holds. Consider a withdraw function that requires the caller to be the owner and checks the balance, then transfers funds and updates state. Emit the Withdrawal event only after the transfer and state update complete. A concrete example: call require for permissions, reduce the contract balance mapping, perform the transfer, and then emit Withdrawal with the recipient, amount, and timestamp. If you emit before the transfer and the transaction reverts, listeners would receive a false signal. Another misconception is to emit events before external calls to save gas in some edge case; this is dangerous because external calls can revert or fail and leave logs inconsistent with on-chain state. Events are not transactional in isolation — they are part of the transaction and will not persist if the transaction reverts, but ordering within the function still affects what you log. End with a simple rule: validate, mutate state, perform external actions, then emit. This pattern makes event logs reliable and trustworthy for off-chain consumers.

keyIdea.title: Emit ordering rule
keyIdea.text: Validate inputs, update state, perform transfers, then emit the event so logs reflect successful changes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Emit Events Safely
Pattern

Validate → Mutate → External → Emit

Follow the sequence to ensure emitted logs describe a committed change.

function withdraw(uint _amount) public {
    require(msg.sender == owner, "Only owner can withdraw.");
    require(address(this).balance >= _amount, "Insufficient balance.");

    // mutate state first
    balances[msg.sender] -= _amount;

    // external action
    payable(msg.sender).transfer(_amount);

    // then emit
    emit Withdrawal(msg.sender, _amount, block.timestamp);
}
Explanation & Example
Concrete example
In withdraw, emitting after transfer prevents false logs when the transfer reverts.
Pitfall
Emitting before state change risks recording actions that never completed if the transaction later fails.
Key Takeaway
Order your function steps so events always reflect the final contract state.

screens.title: Indexed vs Non-indexed Parameters
screens.subtitle: How indexing affects searchability and gas costs

narration.text: Indexed parameters make values searchable because they are stored in topics, which are hashed and optimized for filtering. You can have up to three indexed parameters plus the event signature topic. Non-indexed parameters are placed in the data section and are cheaper to store but not directly filterable by nodes. For example, a Deposit event with address indexed sender and uint amount means you can ask a node to return only Deposit logs where sender equals a particular address. If amount were indexed instead, you could search by amount, but adding indexes increases gas cost. A practical misconception is to index every field 'just in case'. That quickly becomes expensive. Instead, index only keys users or analytics systems will actually query, such as addresses or IDs. Another common confusion is thinking indexing exposes data to contracts; it does not. Both topics and data are public, but indexed fields are simply more easily found by external tools. End with a rule of thumb: index stable, frequently filtered identifiers; leave larger, seldom-filtered payloads as non-indexed data to minimize gas. Indexed vs Non-indexed Parameters means index up to three stable identifiers you will actually filter on; keep larger or rare fields in the data payload to save gas.. In practical terms, how indexing affects searchability and gas costs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Indexing rule of thumb
keyIdea.text: Index up to three stable identifiers you will actually filter on; keep larger or rare fields in the data payload to save gas.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Indexed vs Non-indexed
Indexed (Topics)
Stored as hashed topics enabling fast node-side filtering. Up to three indexed params per event.
Example
Deposit(address indexed sender, uint amount) lets dApps query all Deposit events for a specific sender.
Trade-off
Indexed fields cost more gas. Index only what you will filter by.
Non-indexed (Data)
Stored in the event data payload. Cheaper but not directly searchable; clients must fetch logs then parse the data to filter by those fields.
Example
If amount is non-indexed, a dApp must retrieve Deposit logs and inspect the amount field to find large deposits.
Key Takeaway
Balance index use against gas cost: index identifiers, not every field.

screens.title: Topics, Signature, and Transaction Log Structure
screens.subtitle: How the blockchain stores searchable event metadata

narration.text: Event storage on the blockchain is organized into topics and data. The event signature — its name and parameter types — becomes topic zero. Up to three indexed parameters are hashed into subsequent topics, making them accessible for node-level filtering. The remaining non-indexed parameters are ABI-encoded and stored in the data section of the log entry. This architecture yields a fast path for queries: clients ask nodes for logs matching a signature and specific topic values, and nodes return only matching entries. A concrete example: for event Deposit(address indexed sender, uint amount), topic[0] holds the Deposit signature hash and topic[1] holds the hashed sender address. The amount is in the data section. Tools like Web3 or Ethers call node RPC methods with the event signature and topics to get matching logs. A misconception is that topics reveal raw values; topics are hashed, but because addresses have standard encoding they can be matched efficiently. Finally, remember that logs are not accessible by other contracts; logs exist for external consumers and indexing services. When designing events, consider this storage model and pick fields for topics accordingly to make off-chain filtering efficient.

keyIdea.title: Storage model
keyIdea.text: Events store a signature and up to three indexed topics for fast filtering, with other parameters in the data payload for cheaper storage.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Topics & Log Structure
Architecture
An event log contains the event signature as topic[0], up to three indexed parameter topics, and the ABI-encoded non-indexed data payload. Nodes can filter on topics efficiently.
Topic 0
Event signature hash. Always present for that event type.
Topics 1–3
Hashed indexed parameters used for fast filtering by RPC methods.
Data section
ABI-encoded non-indexed parameters. Clients fetch and decode these after topic-based filtering.
Practical note
Filter by topic for efficiency. To search a non-indexed value requires downloading logs and decoding the data section, which is slower.
Key Takeaway
Design events to expose searchable identifiers in topics and put large payloads in data to control gas cost.

screens.title: Event Use Cases — UI, Analytics, and Off-chain Triggers
screens.subtitle: Common patterns for consuming event logs

narration.text: Events serve three primary off-chain roles. First, user interfaces subscribe to events to update state in real time: a dApp listens for Transfer or Deposit events and refreshes a user's transaction history or balance without repeated polling. Second, analytics platforms and explorers aggregate events to compute metrics, visualize token flows, and present human-friendly histories. Third, off-chain services use events to trigger workflows such as sending notifications or updating traditional databases. A concrete example: a swap contract emits an OrderPlaced event that includes trader, tokenAmount, and price with the trader indexed; a UI can subscribe to show pending orders for a trader, while an analytics system counts orders per token pair. A misconception is to expect events to magically cause on-chain state changes — events are passive and must be acted upon by off-chain agents or a subsequent transaction. Another practical consideration is gas: frequent events are useful but not free. Design events to carry the minimum necessary data for each consumer and let off-chain systems enrich the payload if needed. Ask yourself: which consumers need fast filtering by topic, and which can fetch and decode data when necessary?

keyIdea.title: Three roles
keyIdea.text: Events power real-time UIs, analytics, and off-chain workflows; design them to serve the expected consumers efficiently.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Use Cases
Use cases
UI updates
Subscribe to events like Deposit to update user balances in real time without polling the contract state.
Analytics & explorers
Aggregate Transfer events to produce charts, volume reports, and transaction histories.
Off-chain triggers
Trigger email notifications, database writes, or server-side workflows when events occur.
Scenario
OrderPlaced(trader indexed, tokenAmount, price): index trader for quick account lookup; keep tokenAmount and price in data for cost reasons.
Misconception
Events do not trigger on-chain behavior automatically. They must be read and acted on by off-chain systems or subsequent transactions.
Key Takeaway
Map each event field to its consumer: index searchable keys, keep bulky details in data.

screens.title: Remix Lab Setup — MyToken Starter
screens.subtitle: Prepare the token contract and add TODOs for events

narration.text: In the hands-on activity you'll open Remix IDE and create a file named MyToken. sol with a minimal ERC-20-like token contract. The starter code defines name, symbol, decimals, totalSupply, balances mapping, and simple transfer and approve functions. Your task is to declare Transfer and Approval events and emit them in the corresponding functions. The starter code includes TODO comments where to declare the events and where to emit them. A concrete step sequence is: create the file, paste the starter code, declare events at the top of the contract, add emit Transfer after updating balances in transfer, and emit Approval in approve when the allowance is set or when the function is invoked in the example. Deploy to the JavaScript VM with an initial supply, then call transfer and approve and inspect the logs section in the Remix transaction output. A common oversight is inspecting the wrong transaction; be sure to expand the transaction details and open the logs tab. This lab shows how events appear with topics and data and gives an immediate, visual confirmation that your contract broadcasted the intended actions.

keyIdea.title: Lab goal
keyIdea.text: Declare Transfer and Approval events, emit them in functions, deploy in Remix, and verify logs in the console.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Remix Lab Setup
Starter code
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract MyToken {
    string public name = "My Cohortia Token";
    string public symbol = "MCT";
    uint8 public decimals = 18;
    uint public totalSupply;

    mapping(address => uint) public balances;

    address public owner;

    // TODO: Declare a Transfer event (from, to, amount)
    // TODO: Declare an Approval event (owner, spender, amount)

    constructor(uint _initialSupply) {
        owner = msg.sender;
        totalSupply = _initialSupply * (10 ** uint(decimals));
        balances[owner] = totalSupply;
    }

    function transfer(address _to, uint _value) public returns (bool success) {
        require(balances[msg.sender] >= _value, "Insufficient balance.");
        require(_to != address(0), "Cannot transfer to zero address.");

        balances[msg.sender] -= _value;
        balances[_to] += _value;

        // TODO: Emit the Transfer event
        emit Transfer(msg.sender, _to, _value);
        return true;
    }

    function approve(address _spender, uint _value) public returns (bool success) {
        // TODO: Implement approval logic and emit Approval event
        emit Approval(msg.sender, _spender, _value);
        return true;
    }
}
Lab steps
  1. Create MyToken.sol and paste starter code.
  2. Declare Transfer and Approval events with indexed addresses.
  3. Add emit statements after state updates in transfer and approve.
  4. Deploy to the JavaScript VM and call transfer and approve.
  5. Open the transaction logs in Remix and inspect topics and data.
Tip
Deploy with a small initial supply to make testing transfers simple, and check the logs tab under the transaction details.

screens.title: Implement Transfer & Approval Events
screens.subtitle: Complete the starter token by declaring indexed events

narration.text: In this step you'll implement two canonical ERC-20-like events: Transfer and Approval. The Transfer event typically uses address indexed from, address indexed to, and uint value. The Approval event usually uses address indexed owner, address indexed spender, and uint value. Adding indexed to both address parameters lets explorers quickly find all transfers involving a specific address. Insert these declarations at the top of MyToken. sol. Then, inside transfer after you update balances, call emit Transfer(msg. sender, _to, _value). In approve, emit Approval(msg. sender, _spender, _value) when the allowance is set. A common oversight is to forget to actually update allowances in approve before emitting; in our simplified starter the emit acts as a visible log, but in production you must implement allowance storage changes as well. After deploying and running transfer and approve, open the transaction logs in Remix — the logs will show topic[0] as the event signature and additional topics for the indexed addresses. This is a small but pivotal step: it converts silent state changes into a public, searchable history external systems can consume. Implement Transfer & Approval Events means declare transfer and approval with indexed addresses, emit them after state updates, and verify topics appear in the remix logs.. In practical terms, complete the starter token by declaring indexed events. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Declare Transfer and Approval with indexed addresses, emit them after state updates, and verify topics appear in the Remix logs.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Transfer & Approval
Event declarations
// Declare events
event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint value);
event Approval(address indexed owner, address indexed spender, uint value);
Add these near the top of the contract. Index owner/from/to addresses for efficient filtering by wallets and explorers.
Emit statements
// In transfer()
balances[msg.sender] -= _value;
balances[_to] += _value;
emit Transfer(msg.sender, _to, _value);

// In approve()
// set allowance logic here
emit Approval(msg.sender, _spender, _value);
Key Takeaway
Emitting standard events helps wallets and explorers automatically display transfers and approvals.

narration.text: Events are powerful, but they come with pitfalls. First, never emit sensitive or private data. Logs are public and persist on-chain, so any personal information will be visible to anyone running a node. Second, avoid over-indexing. Each indexed parameter increases gas cost; index only what you expect to filter by frequently, such as user addresses or token IDs. Third, do not expect events to replace on-chain state: other contracts cannot read logs, so events cannot drive on-chain logic. If your contract requires historical data for future decisions, persist needed values in state. Finally, consider gas cost for high-frequency events. Emitting many large events can become expensive over time; store only minimal required information in logs and move heavy processing off-chain. For debugging and auditing, events provide an immutable record, but they are not a safe place to keep secrets. The practical rule is this: use events to broadcast essential, non-sensitive signals that external systems can act upon, and use state for anything contracts themselves must read. Common Mistakes and Safety Notes means avoid logging sensitive data, index sparingly, and use state when on-chain access is required; events are for off-chain listeners.. In practical terms, privacy, gas, and on-chain expectations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safety checklist
keyIdea.text: Avoid logging sensitive data, index sparingly, and use state when on-chain access is required; events are for off-chain listeners.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Common Mistakes
Mistakes
  • Logging private data — logs are public and immutable.
  • Indexing every field — unnecessary indexed params raise gas costs.
  • Relying on events for on-chain logic — contracts cannot read logs.
  • Emitting before state changes — leads to inconsistent or misleading logs if a revert occurs later.
Guidance
Audit your events: ensure they provide necessary info for consumers but avoid excess detail that raises cost or leaks data.
Key Takeaway
Events should be minimal, public-safe, and focused on off-chain consumers; use state for anything contracts must read.

screens.title: Assessment: Choosing Events for a DEX
screens.subtitle: Which logging approach is correct and why

narration.text: Imagine you are building a decentralized exchange and need to signal a new order to UIs and analytics dashboards. The most gas-efficient and appropriate way is to emit an OrderPlaced event with the trader, tokenAmount, and price. Events are specifically designed for off-chain communication and are far cheaper than storing full order histories in contract storage. Storing only the last order in a state variable would waste gas and lose history, and returning details from a function only informs the immediate caller, not all interested listeners. Calling an external contract to store orders introduces additional complexity and cost and still does not offer a general broadcast pattern. When designing the OrderPlaced event, index the trader address so UIs can quickly fetch orders for a specific account and keep larger numeric fields in the data section if you do not need to filter on them. A common misconception is to believe that emitting an event is free; it still costs gas, so balance the level of detail with expected query patterns. Final question: which fields will your front-end need to filter by, and which can live in the data payload?

keyIdea.title: Assessment answer
keyIdea.text: Emit an OrderPlaced event with indexed trader for efficient filtering; avoid storing full histories on-chain to save gas.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Assessment
Question

Best way to signal a new order in a DEX?

Correct choice
Emit OrderPlaced(trader indexed, tokenAmount, price). Index trader for fast account queries; keep numbers in data.
Why not state?
Storing every order in state is expensive and unnecessary for off-chain consumers that can read logs.
Practical prompt
Decide which fields you will query by and index them; otherwise, keep them in data to save gas.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three essential concepts from Events and Logging

narration.text: Let's recap three essential ideas you should retain. First, an event is a contract-level log that is cheaper than state and intended for off-chain consumption; use it to notify UIs and services about important actions. Second, indexed parameters become topics and enable efficient filtering at the node level; limit indexing to the fields you will routinely search for to avoid unnecessary gas costs. Third, events are public and immutable, so never log sensitive data and never expect other contracts to read event logs: events are for external listeners. These three points guide event design: keep events minimal, index thoughtfully, and rely on state for anything the contract itself must read. With these best practices, events become a reliable bridge between on-chain operations and real-world interfaces and tools. Key Concepts — What to Remember means events = off-chain notifications; topics = indexed searchable fields; logs are public — avoid sensitive data.. In practical terms, three essential concepts from events and logging. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Three essentials
keyIdea.text: Events = off-chain notifications; Topics = indexed searchable fields; Logs are public — avoid sensitive data.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Key Concepts
Event
A log entry emitted by a contract to communicate off-chain actions efficiently.
Indexed parameter
Marked with indexed to become a topic, enabling fast filtering by nodes.
Transaction log
Append-only storage of topics and data where event information is recorded.
Summary
Design events to broadcast essential, non-sensitive signals; index only fields you will search often; and verify logs with the Remix console during development.

narration.text: Keep these six compact reminders at hand while designing events. Declare events with the event keyword and emit them after successful state updates. Use indexed to create topics for up to three searchable fields. Place bulky or infrequently queried fields in the data payload to save gas. Never emit sensitive personal data because logs are public and permanent. Finally, remember events are for off-chain consumers; contracts cannot read logs, so persist anything on-chain that other contracts must access. These quick rules will help you design logs that are efficient, private-safe, and easy for UIs and analytic tools to consume. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Key Concepts
Emit after state change
Ensure events reflect committed state to avoid misleading logs.
Index sparingly
Limit indexed params to ones you will actually filter on.
Use topics
Topics enable fast node-side filtering by event signature and indexed parameters.
Save bulky data for data payload
Keep large or rarely-filtered fields in the non-indexed data section to control gas.
Don't log secrets
Event logs are public; never emit private information or secrets.
Events ≠ on-chain state
Contracts cannot read logs; persist values in state if contracts must access them later.
Final note
Use events to bridge on-chain actions to off-chain systems, thoughtfully balancing searchability and cost.
